For one exact layer-height h, a row type consists of floor(S/width) identical complete modules at that fixed frame, centered across a common width S. Its cost is its full row-height, and its value is ab times the module count. A row word with summed heights at most S gives an actual layer with that many whole owners: place the closed row intervals consecutively, center the combined rows, and retain their different module widths. Distinct rows have disjoint box interiors.

A layer word with summed full layer-heights at most S then gives a complete cube packing, by placing those layers on consecutive closed intervals and centering the stack. Different layers have disjoint box interiors. Every owner in a module has the inherited honeycomb orientation, further acted on by the module's fixed proper cube symmetry. The grammar's max-plus count is therefore constructive: its full backpointer word is an inverse decoder, not only an upper or density estimate. All costs lie in (p+q*sqrt(3))/2 with nonnegative integers p,q. The finite dynamic program stores (p,q) costs and an actual word, first for rows at one layer height, then for layers. The metric comparison only orders those exact positive costs against the common cube side; no angle or independent physical scale is optimized.
